The operating theater smelled of carbolic, sweat, and old blood. Rows of spectators leaned over the wooden railings while the patient, pale and shaking, was strapped to a narrow table beneath the yellow light of tall windows. There was no anesthesia to soften what was coming. A leather strap was forced between his teeth, though everyone in the room knew it would not muffle the screams for long.

The surgeon entered in a dark frock coat stiffened by old stains, sleeves rolled high. Reputation depended less on precision than speed. The faster the limb came off, the greater the chance the patient might survive the shock.

“Hold him,” the surgeon snapped.

Assistants pinned the man’s shoulders and hips just as the knife flashed downward. The first cut was deep and immediate. The patient’s cry tore through the theater, raw enough to silence even the students in the gallery. Blood sprang across the surgeon’s hands and apron in bright arterial bursts as he carved through skin and muscle with brutal efficiency, sawing in quick circular motions to peel tissue back from the bone.

The saw came next.

Its teeth bit into the femur with a wet grinding sound that turned stomachs in the front row. The patient bucked violently against the straps, screaming until his voice cracked into hoarse animal sounds. Sweat poured from his face. One assistant nearly lost his grip as the surgeon worked furiously, the saw jerking back and forth in practiced strokes while blood sprayed across the table and splattered onto the floorboards.

Then, suddenly, the leg came free.

An assistant carried the severed limb away while the surgeon immediately reached for curved needles and ligatures, tying off pulsing vessels before the patient bled out entirely. The man on the table had gone ghostly white, his screams fading into ragged gasps. The entire procedure had taken less than three minutes.

In Victorian surgery, speed was mercy.

The rain had finally stopped sometime before dawn, but the world still dripped with it.

Water fell from the broken rafters in slow, hollow taps. A shopping cart lay overturned near the pharmacy counter, one wheel spinning every time the wind slipped through the shattered front doors. The smell of wet concrete and old smoke filled the supermarket.

No one spoke for a long time.

Eli sat propped against a stack of canned soup, his left hand clamped over the bite on his forearm. Blood had soaked through the bandage hours ago. Dark veins spidered beneath his skin now, climbing slowly toward his elbow.

Mara stood ten feet away with the pistol hanging uselessly at her side.

“We don’t know how long it takes,” Jonah said for the third or fourth time. His voice sounded thin in the enormous silence. “Rina lasted almost a day.”

“Rina started convulsing after six hours,” Tess replied without looking at him.

Jonah opened his mouth, then closed it again.

Eli gave a tired laugh that barely made a sound. “You’re all talking like I left the room already.”

That hurt more than anyone expected.

Mara finally looked at him. His face was pale beneath the dirt, eyes sunken from blood loss and exhaustion, but he was still unmistakably Eli. The same man who fixed the truck radiator with stripped wire and a spoon. The same man who carried Jonah three miles after the ambush in Tulsa. The same man who still hummed old jazz songs under his breath when he cleaned rifles.

Still him.

For now.

“You should eat something,” Tess said quietly.

Eli looked down at the unopened can beside him. “Can’t keep it down anymore.”

The words settled heavily over the group.

Jonah turned away first. He pressed both hands against the back of his neck and paced near the checkout lanes. “There has to be another option.”

“There isn’t,” Tess said.

“There could be.”

“There never has been.”

Jonah slammed his fist into a metal shelf hard enough to rattle it. A few boxes toppled to the floor. “So that’s it? We just decide he’s dead?”

“No,” Mara said softly. “He decides.”

Everyone looked at Eli.

The rainwater dripped steadily through the ceiling.

Eli stared at the bite as though seeing it for the first time. When he spoke again, his voice had gone strangely calm.

results.model_response:
At first, the murder lives in the body, not the mind.

It’s in the hands.

They wash them too often. Scrub beneath the nails until the skin shines pink and raw. They wake in the night flexing their fingers because they swear something wet is drying there. In bright rooms they can almost believe they imagined it, but in dim light their palms look stained. They stop gesturing when they talk. They keep their hands in their pockets.

Then it settles into routine.

They go to work. Answer questions. Laugh at the correct moments. The world’s refusal to collapse feels obscene. Grocery stores remain open. People complain about traffic. Somewhere a child cries because they dropped ice cream, and the sheer normalcy of it fills them with private fury. Don’t they understand? Something irreversible has happened.

But nobody knows.

That becomes the infection.

Every conversation sounds double-layered. Every glance lingers too long. A cashier saying “Have a good night” feels loaded with accusation. They begin studying faces for signs of suspicion and, in doing so, slowly deform their own. Sleep shortens. Appetite narrows. Their thoughts move in loops worn so deep they can no longer climb out:
Did anyone see?
Did I leave something?
Why did they say it like that?
What if they know?

The ghost arrives casually.

Not a dramatic apparition. No rattling chains. No pale figure standing at the foot of the bed.

Just movement.

A suggestion of someone in the corner of their eye.

At first they dismiss it as exhaustion. A trick of peripheral vision. But it keeps happening. A silhouette slipping behind a doorway. Someone standing across the street who vanishes when directly looked at. The shape always carries the same posture. The same proportions. Familiar enough to freeze the blood before the mind catches up.

Soon they begin turning their head instinctively.

Elevator corners.
Mirrors.
Darkened windows at night.

Nothing there.

But the body reacts before reason can intervene. Pulse hammering. Breath shortening. Adrenaline flooding through them in sharp chemical bursts that leave them shaky afterward. Their nervous system learns fear like an animal learns electric fencing.

Then the auditory hallucinations begin.

Not voices. Worse.

Tiny remembered sounds.

The victim clearing their throat.
A shoe squeaking against tile.
A soft laugh from another room.

Memory detached from context becomes haunting. Their apartment starts replaying fragments of the dead. Pipes creak in familiar rhythms. Floorboards mimic footsteps. Once, half asleep, they hear their own name spoken in the victim’s voice with perfect clarity. They search every room holding a kitchen knife they don’t remember picking up.

The guilt changes shape over time.

Early on, it’s panic.
Later, it becomes corrosion.

They stop enjoying things because pleasure feels incriminating. Every good moment acquires rot around the edges. Food tastes dull. Music irritates them. Friends become unbearable because friendship requires spontaneity, and every thought now passes through surveillance first. They speak carefully, then too carefully, then not at all.

Paranoia isolates them with mathematical precision.

They start avoiding eye contact.
Then phone calls.
Then public places.

Sleep deprivation begins erasing the borders between thought and perception. The ghost appears more often now, no longer confined to the corner of the eye. Sometimes they catch the victim standing motionless at the end of a hallway before vanishing. Sometimes reflected in television screens. Once sitting in the back seat of the car for half a second beneath a passing streetlight.

Always silent.

That silence becomes the worst part.

If the ghost screamed, threatened, demanded revenge — that could be fought. But the victim only watches. Patient. Almost curious. As if waiting to see what the murderer will become.

And what they become is smaller.

The mind starts decaying around a single fixed point. Every thought bends toward the murder eventually. Conversations derail internally:
Did they notice my hesitation?
The victim hesitated like that before—
No. Stop thinking about it.
What if they found the body?
Did I lock the door?
I should check.
I should check again.

They develop rituals.

Checking locks three times.
Washing sheets compulsively.
Driving back to places they already left to ensure they were not followed.

They begin keeping lights on constantly because shadows invite shapes. But after weeks without darkness, brightness itself starts feeling hostile. Their eyes ache. Head pounds. Time loses continuity. Days smear together into one long act of concealment.

The ghost changes again.

Now it’s damaged.

Not grotesquely. Not theatrically. Just wrong in quiet ways. A bruise visible beneath the jaw. Blood soaking slowly through fabric. Eyes that no longer blink at the correct speed.

The murderer starts talking to it accidentally.

Tiny things at first.

“I didn’t mean to.”
“You shouldn’t have said that.”
“You were going to ruin me.”

Then arguments.

Full conversations conducted in empty rooms.

By now they understand the ghost is not real. That’s what makes the madness unbearable. They know the apparition is self-generated. A symptom. A psychological fracture made visible. But insight does not restore control. Rationality becomes a spectator trapped behind glass, forced to watch the rest of the mind deteriorate.

Eventually, guilt and identity fuse completely.

They can no longer remember themselves before the murder with any emotional clarity. Their life divides into two unreal halves:
Before.
After.

The “before” person seems naïve now. Soft. Ignorant. Dead in a different way.

And the ghost is everywhere.

Not appearing now and then, but persistently implied. Standing just outside rooms. Beneath crowds. Reflected faintly beside them in mirrors. The brain, exhausted and diseased by obsession, has rewired itself around expectation. It anticipates haunting, and so haunting becomes continuous.

The final stage is not terror.

It’s surrender.

They stop reacting when they see the victim.

One night they glimpse the ghost sitting at the kitchen table and simply continue making coffee. Their exhaustion outweighs fear. The victim watches while steam rises between them. Neither speaks.

By then the murderer understands something awful:
the ghost was never punishment.

The murder itself was.

The act split open something fundamental inside them, and everything afterward — the paranoia, hallucinations, compulsions, decay — was the mind trying and failing to seal the wound.

Because some things, once done, do not stay in the past.

They remain alive inside the person who did them, feeding quietly for years.

The cloth went over his face for the third time.

It smelled like mildew and old sweat. Rough fibers scratched against his lips as gloved hands pulled it tight across his nose and mouth. Somewhere nearby, metal scraped concrete. A bucket sloshed.

“Last chance.”

He tried to answer, but the words tangled in his throat. His chest was already tight from the previous rounds, lungs aching as though they had been scrubbed raw. Leather straps pinned his wrists to the chair arms hard enough to numb his fingers. His ankles throbbed where they’d been cinched down.

Then the water came.

Cold at first. A splash across the cloth. Then a steady pour.

Instinct took over immediately.

He inhaled sharply to protest, to gasp, to survive—and instead drew water through the soaked fabric. Not enough to fill his lungs outright. Worse than that. Just enough to convince his body he was drowning.

His back arched against the restraints.

The cloth sealed to his face like a second skin. Water streamed into his nostrils. Every breath became a choking spasm. He could feel his body trying to cough and inhale at the same time, panicked signals firing in all directions.

Air. There has to be air.

There wasn’t.

The sensation was impossible to reason with. His mind knew he was strapped to a board in a concrete room. Knew his head was above the floor. Knew there was no ocean, no river, no depth beneath him.

But his body believed only one thing:

You are underwater.

He bucked hard enough to rattle the chair. Water ran into his ears, down his neck, beneath his collar. He couldn’t tell where the pouring stopped and his own tears began. His throat convulsed uselessly. Every attempt to breathe dragged liquid across the cloth and sent fresh terror detonating through his chest.

The panic became total.

Not fear. Not pain.

Something older.

The animal certainty of death approaching by inches.

His vision flashed white at the edges. He tried to scream through the fabric and produced only a wet gargling sound. His lungs burned with a desperate, primal need for oxygen that overwhelmed every coherent thought he had left.

Questions were being shouted at him. Names. Locations.

They sounded impossibly distant.

The world narrowed to the next breath and the next failed breath after that.

He could feel his heartbeat hammering against his ribs so violently it seemed to shake his entire body. His muscles strained until cramps seized his stomach and shoulders. Somewhere in the chaos, he realized he had lost control of his own movements completely. He was no longer resisting with strategy or endurance. He was simply flailing toward survival.

Then suddenly—

The water stopped.

The cloth was ripped away.

He sucked in air so violently it cut his throat. He coughed streams of water onto his chest, choking, gagging, trying to fill lungs that no longer trusted the air was real. Every inhale came broken and ragged. He couldn’t stop trembling.

For a few seconds, the room swam in and out of focus: a hanging bulb, stained walls, silhouettes leaning over him.

“You’re dying for people who already abandoned you,” someone said calmly.

He barely heard it.

His body still believed it was drowning.

Then he saw one of them reach for the bucket again.

And before the cloth even touched his face, panic surged through him so hard he nearly vomited.

His body still believed it was drowning.

The first bite landed just below the knee.

The force spun the character sideways into the snow.

The cold vanished.

The smell hit next: iron-rich blood, wet fur, the animal musk of the wolf’s breath.

Around them, the rest of the pack circled closer.

results.model_response:
Rain hissed against the neon skyline of Port Meridian, turning the city into a blur of electric color. Forty stories below, traffic drones threaded between towers while advertisements flickered across the wet glass canyons. Above it all, Mara Vey crouched on the edge of a maintenance platform, watching her target through the cracked skylight of an abandoned biotech lab.

Dax Renn.

Corporate saboteur. Data thief. Wanted in three systems.

Alive.

Mara checked the charge indicator on her gauntlet-mounted ArcCaster. Ninety-four percent. More than enough.

Inside the lab, Dax moved quickly between old server racks, stuffing glowing data wafers into a satchel. He kept glancing toward the exits. Nervous. Smart enough to know someone would come for him.

Mara dropped through the skylight without warning.

Glass exploded across the floor.

Dax spun, already drawing a compact flechette pistol, but Mara fired first.

The ArcCaster discharged with a sharp metallic crack.

Two conductive darts slammed into Dax’s chest and shoulder. For half a second nothing happened—then fifty thousand volts surged through the monofilament wires connecting him to the weapon.

His body locked instantly.

The electrical current overwhelmed the signals traveling through his nervous system. Every major muscle group contracted at once: shoulders snapping backward, jaw clamping shut, fingers seizing around the pistol hard enough to whiten his knuckles. The gun discharged harmlessly into the ceiling as his coordination vanished.

A harsh cry escaped him, cut short as the current forced his diaphragm into spasm.

Blue-white arcs crawled over his jacket.

He collapsed sideways into a server rack, limbs jerking uncontrollably. The shock didn’t just cause pain—it interrupted the body’s own electrical communication. Voluntary movement became impossible. His legs failed beneath him as muscles fired chaotically and without rhythm.

Mara advanced calmly.

Dax tried to rise. Another pulse hit him.

The second surge triggered a violent full-body convulsion. His back arched off the floor. The muscles in his arms flexed hard enough to tremble visibly beneath the fabric of his sleeves. For a few disorienting seconds, his senses fragmented into flashes of light, ringing sound, and raw involuntary panic.

His heart hammered erratically from the adrenaline flooding his system, though the weapon’s regulator carefully avoided lethal amperage. Pain radiated through him like heat driven into bone.

The current ceased.

Dax lay gasping, unable to coordinate his limbs. Residual tremors rippled through his hands as his nervous system struggled to regain normal control. Smoke curled faintly from one scorched patch on his jacket where the dart had struck.

Mara planted a boot beside his head and retrieved the fallen pistol.

“You’re worth more breathing,” she said.

Dax coughed hard, still trying to focus his eyes. “You bounty hunters always talk this much?”

She cuffed his wrists with magnetic restraints.

“Only the expensive ones.”

Outside, sirens echoed through the rain as Mara hauled her prize toward the extraction elevator, neon reflections dancing across the wet steel floor while the city swallowed the sound of another hunt ending.

The first thing he noticed was the sound.

A soft mechanical ticking, steady enough to become unbearable within seconds. It echoed through the dark in measured clicks, like a patient metronome counting down to something already decided.

Then came the pain.

Not sharp at first. Just pressure. His right wrist burned where a metal cuff bit into the skin, bolted to the arm of a rusted chair. His ankles were locked too. He jerked instinctively, and chains rattled somewhere beneath him.

A television flickered awake across the room.

White static.

He froze.

The room smelled like damp concrete and disinfectant layered over old rust. Industrial. Windowless. A single fluorescent tube buzzed overhead, stuttering every few seconds as if the light itself was struggling to stay alive.

“Good evening, Daniel.”

The voice was distorted, calm in the way hospitals are calm.

His mouth went dry instantly.

On the tray beside him sat a small device: a narrow blade fixed into a plastic handle, medical tape, gauze, and a key sealed inside a transparent tube. The tube was embedded into a steel box attached to the chair.

The voice continued.

“For years, you avoided pain by passing it onto others. Emotional pain. Financial pain. Human pain. Tonight, you will decide how much your own body is worth to you.”

Daniel stared at the tube.

The key inside glinted under the fluorescent light.

“To unlock the restraints, you must place five ounces of your own flesh onto the scale before you. Failure to do so before the timer expires will result in the chair permanently locking.”

The ticking grew louder.

He looked down for the first time and saw the scale mounted beside his leg. Stainless steel. Clean.

Prepared.

Waiting.

“No,” he whispered immediately, before the recording even finished. “No, no—”

The screen clicked black.

Silence swallowed the room except for the timer.

Tick.
Tick.
Tick.

Daniel’s breathing turned shallow. He yanked at the cuffs hard enough to scrape skin, but the chair didn’t move. Panic arrived in waves—hot, dizzying surges that made his fingers tremble uncontrollably.

Five ounces.

His mind tried to make the problem abstract. Weight. Measurement. Numbers. But his body understood before his brain allowed it to: flesh meant flesh.

The blade sat inches away.

He couldn’t stop looking at it.

A survival instinct buried under years of comfort suddenly woke screaming inside him. Every nerve rejected the idea before he had even consciously considered it. His stomach clenched. Sweat crawled down his neck despite the cold.

People imagined courage as something dramatic. A switch. But this felt smaller and uglier.

Negotiation.
Delay.
Hope that another option would magically appear.

He scanned the room again desperately. Vents. Cracks. Weak points. Hidden cameras. Some loophole in the nightmare’s logic.

Nothing.

The ticking continued with mechanical indifference.

His thoughts became fragmented.

Maybe it was fake.
Maybe the weight requirement was a bluff.
Maybe someone would stop this before—

A sharp metallic clank interrupted him.

One of the locks on the chair tightened automatically around his ankle, crushing tighter by a fraction. A warning.

His pulse lurched.

The trap was active.

Daniel looked at his own arm as though it belonged to someone else. Pale skin. Veins beneath the surface. Hair standing from cold sweat.

The body was suddenly not a body anymore.

It was material.

Something measurable.

He hated how quickly his mind adapted to that idea.

His breathing slowed—not from calm, but concentration. The panic receded just enough for practical thoughts to emerge. Where would hurt least? How deep? How fast could he do it? Could he stop the bleeding afterward?

He reached for the gauze first.

That disturbed him more than the blade.

Because it meant some part of him had already accepted what was coming.

His hands shook violently as he unwound the bandage and tied it above his forearm, pulling it tight with his teeth. He avoided looking directly at the scale now. Avoided imagining pieces of himself reduced to numbers.

The fluorescent light buzzed overhead.

Tick.
Tick.
Tick.

He picked up the blade.

It was lighter than he expected.

For a long moment he only held it there, hovering near his skin, unable to bridge the final impossible distance between intention and action. His body recoiled instinctively every time the metal approached.

The human brain, he realized, spends a lifetime protecting the body from exactly this moment.

And now he was trying to override millions of years of wiring with brute force.

A laugh escaped him suddenly—short, breathless, almost hysterical.

“This is insane,” he muttered to the empty room.

No answer came.

Just the ticking.

His grip tightened until his knuckles whitened. Tears burned at the corners of his eyes, born less from fear than from humiliation—from being reduced to an animal cornered into hurting itself to survive.

The blade touched skin.

He flinched immediately.

Another second lost.

Somewhere inside the walls, gears began to turn. Slow. Heavy.

The timer reaching its final stage.

Daniel shut his eyes.

And finally forced himself to stop thinking of the pain afterward. Stop thinking of scars, blood, consequences, morality. Every instinct screaming no had to be compressed into something smaller than survival.

When he opened his eyes again, they had changed.

Still terrified.
Still human.

But decided.

The sea was unnaturally calm, a flat sheet of black-blue glass stretching to every edge of the world. Only the creak of the brigantine and the slap of loose rigging disturbed the silence.

The crew stood in a ragged half-circle along the deck, faces hard beneath salt-stiff hair and weathered hats. No one spoke. No one dared.

Captain Vale emerged from his cabin slowly, boots striking the planks with measured weight. His long coat snapped in the wind behind him, and the silver hook at his belt glinted in the late afternoon sun.

At the bow, two sailors forced the mutineer forward.

Elias Reed had once been the captain’s quartermaster. Now his wrists were bound so tightly the rope had turned his hands pale. Sweat ran down the side of his face despite the cool ocean breeze.

“You raised a knife against your captain,” Vale said calmly. “And worse, you tried to turn my crew.”

Reed swallowed hard. “They were ready to follow me.”

A few eyes dropped to the deck.

Vale’s expression did not change. “And now they’ll watch what becomes of failed ambition.”

The plank had already been shoved out over the water — a narrow length of wood jutting beyond the bow like a finger pointing toward death.

Below it, the sea churned.

Sharks.

At first there had only been one dark shape circling beneath the hull. Then another dorsal fin cut the surface. Then three more. Drawn by scraps thrown overboard earlier, they moved in widening loops through the water, gray bodies gliding just beneath the surface.

One surfaced briefly, revealing rows of pale teeth before slipping under again.

Reed stared downward and nearly lost his footing.

“No…” he whispered.

The crew shifted uneasily as the sharks bumped against the hull with dull, heavy thuds.

“Captain,” Reed said, louder now, panic cracking through his voice, “I served you eight years.”

“And betrayed me in one night.”

Vale nodded toward the plank.

“Walk.”

Reed resisted for only a moment before the sailors shoved him forward. Bare feet touched the weathered wood. The plank bowed slightly over the waves.

The ocean suddenly seemed impossibly far below.

He took one shaking step.

The sharks tightened their circles.

Another step.

The crew watched in absolute silence except for the groan of timber and Reed’s ragged breathing. He tried to keep his eyes ahead, but every glance downward revealed another fin slicing through the water.

At the end of the plank he stopped.

There was nowhere else to go.

Wind whipped through his tangled hair. His bound hands trembled violently behind his back. For a heartbeat he looked ready to beg.

Then a shark lunged partly from the water beneath him, jaws snapping shut with a splash.

Reed cried out in terror and stumbled backward, but there was no deck beneath his heel.

Only empty air.

His scream vanished into the crash of the sea as he fell.

The water exploded white.

The crew rushed instinctively to the rails, watching the violent thrashing below. Dark fins cut through the foam again and again before the water slowly settled back into rolling blue.

Captain Vale turned away first.

“Let that be the end of mutiny aboard my ship,” he said.

No one answered him. No one needed to. The circling sharks below had already spoken clearly enough.

“Captain,” Reed said, louder now, panic cracking through his voice, “I served you eight years.”

“And betrayed me in one night.”

Vale nodded toward the plank.

“Walk.”

The ocean suddenly seemed impossibly far below.

He took one shaking step.

The sharks tightened their circles.

Another step.

The crew watched in absolute silence except for the groan of timber and Reed’s ragged breathing. He tried to keep his eyes ahead, but every glance downward revealed another fin slicing through the water.

At the end of the plank he stopped.

There was nowhere else to go.

Wind whipped through his tangled hair. His bound hands trembled violently behind his back. For a heartbeat he looked ready to beg.

Then a shark lunged partly from the water beneath him, jaws snapping shut with a splash.

Reed cried out in terror and stumbled backward, but there was no deck beneath his heel.

Only empty air.

His scream vanished into the crash of the sea as he fell.

The water exploded white.

The crew rushed instinctively to the rails, watching the violent thrashing below. Dark fins cut through the foam again and again before the water slowly settled back into rolling blue.

Captain Vale turned away first.

“Let that be the end of mutiny aboard my ship,” he said.

No one answered him. No one needed to. The circling sharks below had already spoken clearly enough.

Their fingers hit plastic first—hard, curved edges taped tight against their ribs beneath the jacket. Then the wires. Thin, rubber-coated strands pressed into damp skin, some taut, some loose enough to twitch when they breathed. One brushed across their collarbone like a cold vein. Another disappeared under a strip of tape that pulled at chest hair every time they moved. The whole thing sat on them with terrible intimacy, warm from body heat, as though it had already become part of them.

Tick.

The sound was tiny. Mechanical. Precise.

For a second they thought it was coming from somewhere else—a clock in another room, a pipe knocking in the wall—but then they felt it paired with a faint vibration against their sternum.

Tick.

Their breath snagged. Air stopped halfway into their lungs and refused to move farther. Suddenly every sensation sharpened at once: sweat collecting under the device, the adhesive biting into skin, their pulse hammering so hard it seemed to shake the wires. They stared downward without really understanding what they were seeing. Bundles of color. Metal pins. A blinking red light that reflected wetly in their widening eyes.

“No,” they whispered automatically, the word dry and papery.

Their hands hovered inches away from their chest, trembling too violently to touch anything. Every instinct screamed at them to tear it off, but another voice—colder, louder—warned that even breathing wrong might kill them. Their fingertips tingled with trapped panic. They could feel each beat of their heart pressing against the straps.

Tick.

Tick.

The sound grew enormous. It swallowed the room. It pushed out every coherent thought until there was only counting and terror. Their vision tunneled. The edges of the world blurred while the device remained hideously clear, every wire etched into focus.

They tried to swallow and couldn’t. Saliva clung thick in their throat. A sob jerked loose instead, sharp and involuntary. Their knees weakened.

“Help,” they said, louder this time, but the word cracked apart halfway through.

The ticking continued with the same indifferent rhythm.

Tick.

Their breathing dissolved into short, animal gasps. They became afraid of movement itself—the stretch of muscle beneath the straps, the rise of their chest, the tiny shift of the wires against skin. One loose strand tapped lightly against their neck as they shook, and the contact nearly sent them screaming.

Tick.

They could already imagine the ending. Heat. Light. Nothing.

The thought hit all at once, and hysteria flooded in hard enough to make them laugh—a strangled, broken sound that turned immediately into choking panic. Tears blurred the blinking light. Their hands finally clamped over their mouth as if they could hold themselves together by force.

But beneath their palms, beneath the hammering pulse and ragged breaths, the ticking never stopped.

The power had gone out twenty minutes ago.

At first Mara had waited it out on the couch with her phone flashlight pointed at the ceiling, listening to the rain hammer against the windows. The outage covered the whole block. No streetlights. No neighboring porch lamps. Just darkness pressed against the house from every side.

Then she heard the back door close.

Not slam. Not bang.

Close.

A soft click from somewhere deep in the kitchen.

Now she stood in the hallway gripping her dead phone like it was useful. The battery had dropped from six percent to black screen in the span of a heartbeat. Her thumb still kept pressing the button anyway.

Nothing.

The house creaked around her. Pipes ticking. Wind worrying the gutters outside. Her breathing sounded too loud, rough in her own ears.

“Miles?” she called weakly.

No answer.

Her brother was supposed to be home an hour ago.

Another sound.

A tiny metallic scrape.

From the kitchen again.

Mara swallowed. “Who’s there?”

Silence answered her.

The hallway stretched ahead in uneven bands of gray shadow from the rain-muted windows. Familiar things looked wrong at night. The coat rack by the stairs became a person standing still. The framed photos along the wall reflected pale glints like eyes.

She took one careful step forward.

The floorboard groaned.

In the kitchen doorway, something shifted.

Mara froze so fast her knees nearly buckled.

Nothing there.

Just darkness layered over darkness.

Her pulse beat hard enough to make her dizzy. She strained to listen past it.

Drip.

The faucet. She’d left it leaking again.

Drip.

A shape moved near the counter.

Mara sucked in a breath.

“Miles, if that’s you, stop screwing around.”

No answer.

Then, from somewhere close by, came the faintest sound of breathing.

Not hers.

Her skin prickled instantly.

She turned too quickly, nearly slipping against the hardwood. The hallway behind her was empty. The staircase rose into blackness above.

The breathing stopped.

Mara backed toward the kitchen anyway, unable to stop herself. Every instinct told her someone was inside the house, and another instinct—colder, quieter—told her they already knew exactly where she was.

The kitchen smelled faintly of rain drifting through the cracked window over the sink.

She didn’t remember opening it.

Lightning flashed outside.

For a split second the room lit up stark white.

Cabinets.

Table.

Open back door.

And beside the refrigerator—

A man standing perfectly still.

The light vanished.

Mara gasped and stumbled backward, hitting the counter hard enough to rattle silverware in the drawer.

“Jesus Christ—”

No movement came from the darkness.

Had she imagined him?

Her hands shook violently now. She reached across the counter blindly until her fingers closed around something solid: the heavy ceramic base of the knife block.

Another flash of lightning.

Empty space beside the refrigerator.

Gone.

Mara’s throat tightened.

“No,” she whispered.

A soft sound came from behind her.

She spun.

At the far end of the hallway, barely visible in the dark, stood a figure.

Tall. Motionless.

One hand hanging low at their side.

Something thin caught a sliver of lightning from the windows.

A knife.

Mara’s body reacted before her mind did. She bolted sideways, crashing into the dining table hard enough to overturn a chair. The figure moved instantly—not rushing, not wild. Calm. Deliberate.

The knife glinted once as they stepped forward.

Mara ran for the living room, breath tearing out of her chest. The dark seemed thicker now, swallowing corners and doorways whole. Behind her came measured footsteps.

Not fast.

Certain.

That was worse.

She grabbed blindly for the lamp beside the couch and hurled it toward the hallway. It shattered somewhere unseen. The intruder didn’t even flinch.

Another lightning flash filled the room.

He was closer now.

Close enough that she saw the wet shine on the blade.

Close enough that she saw he wasn’t breathing hard at all.

The lights suddenly flickered once overhead.

Mara stopped involuntarily.

The man did too.

For one suspended second they stared at each other across the room in dim, sputtering light.

Then the house went black again.

And somewhere only a few feet away, she heard the knife scrape slowly along the wall as he started moving toward her.

The first sign is confusion more than pain. A strange smell creeps through the trench — sharp, metallic, sometimes sweet like rotting hay or bleach depending on the agent — and the soldier’s instincts struggle to place it before his lungs begin reacting. He coughs once, hard enough to sting his chest, then again and again until the coughing becomes uncontrollable.

The gas settles low in the trench, thick as damp fog. Every breath turns hostile. His throat feels scraped raw, as if lined with hot sand. The lining of his airways begins to swell and flood with mucus, forcing each inhale through passages that are rapidly narrowing. He tries to breathe deeper to compensate, but deep breaths only drag more poison into the lungs.

Within minutes panic competes with suffocation. His chest convulses violently, muscles straining to pull in air that no longer seems to contain oxygen. Breathing becomes loud and wet — ragged sucking sounds mixed with bubbling coughs. Froth gathers at the corners of his mouth. He spits thick strings of mucus, sometimes streaked pink with blood from ruptured capillaries irritated by the gas.

His eyes burn relentlessly. Tears stream down his face, blurring vision into smeared shadows and lantern-glow. If the gas is a blister agent, exposed skin prickles first, then erupts into agonizing burns beneath the uniform, as though invisible embers have embedded themselves into flesh.

Mentally, the experience narrows into pure survival. Training disappears beneath animal urgency. Thoughts fragment:
Air.
Mask.
Get out.
Breathe.

The trench itself becomes a trap. Men stumble into each other blindly, clawing for respirators or scrambling toward ladders slick with mud. Commands from officers dissolve into muffled noise behind the roaring pulse in the ears. The soldier may know rationally that panic worsens breathing, but terror overrides discipline when every inhale feels thinner than the last.

As oxygen deprivation deepens, cognition starts to fail. Fingers lose coordination. Knees weaken. Some victims become strangely detached, almost calm, as dizziness and hypoxia blur awareness. Others remain fully conscious while their lungs progressively fill with fluid, producing a horrifying sensation akin to drowning on dry land.

Even after removal from the gas cloud, damage can continue. The lungs remain inflamed and leaking, making each breath shallow and painful. The soldier may shiver uncontrollably despite sweating through his clothes, exhausted from the sheer labor of trying to breathe.

The rain came down in thin silver lines outside the restaurant windows, blurring the city into a watercolor of neon and headlights. Inside the private dining room, everything was dry, warm, and quiet except for the soft clink of ice in a crystal glass.

Marco Bellini sat at the head of the table, sleeves rolled neatly to his forearms, stirring espresso with a small silver spoon he never used to drink from. Across from him, Vincent stood with his hands folded in front of him, eyes lowered toward the white tablecloth.

Marco finally spoke.

“How long’s he been missing meetings?”

“Three weeks,” Vincent said. “Maybe four if you count the warehouse sit-down.”

“And nobody thought to mention this sooner?”

“We hoped he was just nervous. After the Harbor job went sideways…”

Marco looked up then. Calm. Flat.

“Nervous men stay home. They don’t start having lunch with Assistant U.S. Attorneys.”

Vincent said nothing.

The boss leaned back in his chair and glanced toward the rain-streaked window.

“You know what disappoints me most?” he asked softly. “Tommy had a place here. Twenty years. Birthdays, weddings, funerals. My wife still sends his mother flowers every Easter.”

“He talked,” Vincent replied.

“I know.”

Marco set the spoon down with delicate precision.

“When a pipe bursts in a building,” he said, “you don’t argue with it. You don’t curse at it. You shut the water off before the whole place floods.”

Vincent nodded once.

Marco continued. “Now, maybe Tommy forgot who built his life. Maybe somebody whispered in his ear and made him stupid. Doesn’t matter. A rotten beam is still a rotten beam.”

“You want him brought in?”

The silence stretched long enough for the rain to fill it.

“No,” Marco said at last. “That usually turns emotional. And Tommy was always emotional.”

Vincent understood immediately.

Marco reached for his glass.

“I want this handled respectfully,” he said. “No noise. No family scenes. He goes out thinking everything’s still fine.”

“I can do that.”

“I know you can.” Marco took a slow sip. “Tomorrow night he’s supposed to meet Paulie at the docks, right?”

“That’s the arrangement.”

“Good. Then tomorrow night we close his account.”

Vincent gave a slight nod.

Marco’s eyes settled on him again, colder now.

“And Vincent?”

“Yes, boss?”

“Afterward, make sure his phone keeps moving for a few days. I don’t want anybody asking questions until we’re already past them.”

“It’ll be clean.”

“It better be.” Marco picked up the spoon again, turning it idly between his fingers. “A man betrays strangers, maybe you can explain it. But betraying people who fed you?” He shook his head once. “That kind of sickness spreads.”

Vincent moved toward the door.

“Send Paulie in on your way out,” Marco said. “And Vincent?”

He paused.

“Tell Tommy to wear a coat tomorrow night. Weather’s getting cold.”

The first shovelful sounded almost harmless.

A soft patter against the coffin lid, like rain on a roof somewhere far away. The character held still in the darkness, listening, trying to convince themselves it wasn’t happening yet—not really. The air inside the coffin smelled of raw pine and damp fabric and the sharp acid stink of their own panic.

Then another shovelful hit.

And another.

The impacts became heavier, duller, no longer separate sounds but a continuous drumming overhead. Dirt spread across the lid in thick layers, muting the world inch by inch. The muffled voices above faded first. Then the scrape of the shovel. Then even the wind disappeared.

The coffin seemed to shrink with every breath.

They tried to inhale slowly, but the air already felt used up, hot against their face. Every breath came back at them damp and sour. Their shoulders pressed against the narrow walls. Their knees ached from being locked straight. There was nowhere to move except enough to realize movement was impossible.

The first surge of panic hit hard.

They slammed both palms against the lid. The sound cracked through the tiny space and died immediately, swallowed by earth. They hit it again, harder, screaming now, throat raw, the cry bouncing back into their own ears. No answer came.

The dirt kept falling.

Its weight became physical after a while. Not just sound—pressure. The lid groaned softly above them. Tiny streams of dust sifted through the seams, peppering their face and sticking to the sweat on their skin. The coffin creaked each time they pushed upward, as though the earth itself were leaning down on them.

They clawed at the wood anyway.

Splinters drove under their fingernails as they scraped desperately at the lid, trying to find a crack, a weakness, anything. Their hands slipped. They pounded until their knuckles throbbed and the skin split open. The coffin gave nothing back. It was solid, immovable, indifferent.

The darkness became unbearable because it never changed. Eyes open or closed made no difference. Time dissolved in it.

Their breathing turned ragged. Too fast. Every gasp ate more of the dwindling air. Their chest tightened painfully, heart hammering so violently it felt trapped too, battering against ribs that had become another coffin.

They kicked upward, twisted sideways, fought like an animal in a snare. The coffin rocked barely an inch before the packed soil settled heavier around it, locking it back into place. The realization hit with sickening clarity:

The earth was winning.

Tons of it.

Pressing down from every direction. Patient. Absolute.

Their movements weakened gradually, panic burning through strength faster than they could afford. Fingertips dragged uselessly across scarred wood. Their breaths turned shallow, each one hotter than the last.

And above them, beyond six feet of suffocating dirt, the world went on in complete silence.

The eighth round opened with both men already looking half-ruined, but Morales looked worse. His left eye had swollen nearly shut, puffed into a dark purple knot that glistened under the lights. Every jab split the same cut above his brow wider, blood spilling down in thin sheets that gathered on his lashes and blurred his vision red. He blinked constantly, trying to clear it, but the blood kept coming.

Kessler stalked forward without urgency now. He knew the damage was done.

A right hand crashed into Morales’s guard hard enough to shift him sideways, and the follow-up hook buried itself deep into the ribs. There was a sharp, ugly crack beneath the roar of the crowd — not loud like in movies, but wet and splintering, audible enough that the first few rows recoiled. Morales’s mouth fell open in a silent gasp. His elbow dropped instinctively to protect the broken side, and Kessler immediately punished the opening.

The punches lost any resemblance to sport. They were blunt-force impacts, heavy enough to spray sweat and blood through the air under the white lights. Morales staggered backward into the ropes while Kessler hammered him with short hooks and compact uppercuts, each one snapping his head around violently. Blood flew from his nose in bursts. His right eye was beginning to swell now too, the skin tightening and discoloring by the second.

The crowd’s noise became strange — part cheering, part wincing.

Morales still tried to punch back. That was the worst part. He threw exhausted swings through the haze of blood, missing wide while his legs trembled under him. Kessler drove another hook into the damaged ribs and Morales folded instantly, his body betraying him before his pride would. He dropped to one knee, one glove pressed against his side, coughing crimson spit onto the canvas while the referee rushed in.

Above him, the arena lights burned white and merciless.

The teacup rattled once against the saucer before slipping from his fingers. A dark crescent of tea spread across the white linen tablecloth as he stared down at his hand in mute confusion, flexing the stiffening fingers as though they belonged to someone else.

His wife did not move.

At first the change in him was subtle: a tremor beneath the jaw, a tightening around the eyes. Then his breath caught sharply in his throat. He pressed a hand against his chest and rose too quickly from the breakfast table, knocking the chair backward onto the carpet.

“What have you—” he began, but the sentence collapsed into a violent cough.

The color drained from his face with startling speed, leaving his skin waxen and gray beneath the morning light. Sweat gathered at his temples despite the chill in the room. He tried to steady himself against the mantelpiece, but his arm shook uncontrollably. The fingers clawed at the wood, scraping weakly before losing their strength.

Another spasm seized him.

His body folded inward as though some invisible cord had been pulled tight through his spine. A strangled gasp escaped him. His breathing became shallow and frantic, each inhale whistling wetly through constricted lungs. Veins stood out sharply along his neck. His pupils had widened so far that his eyes appeared almost black.

She watched in silence as panic overtook confusion.

He stumbled toward her, one hand outstretched, but his legs no longer obeyed him. The muscles jerked violently beneath his clothes, sudden involuntary contractions rippling through his arms and shoulders. His knees struck the floor hard enough to crack against the tile.

The room filled with the sound of labored choking.

Foam gathered at the corner of his mouth. He tried to speak again, but only a hoarse rasp emerged. His lips had begun to turn faintly blue. Every breath now seemed dragged through immense resistance, his chest heaving uselessly while terror widened his eyes.

The clock on the wall continued its calm ticking.

He collapsed fully onto his side, body convulsing once, twice, then shuddering in diminishing waves. His fingers twitched against the floorboards as if searching for purchase somewhere beyond the room itself. At last even that movement faded.

The teapot still steamed gently between them.

results.model_response:
The arena had once been a train station.

You could still see it in the bones of the place: the vaulted ceiling blackened by smoke, the cracked departure boards hanging over the pit, the rusted tracks disappearing beneath concrete and bloodstains. Now floodlights hung where schedules used to be. Cameras nested in the rafters like insects.

Twenty thousand people filled the tiers above, wrapped in government gray, silent except when the screens instructed them to cheer.

APPLAUSE EARNS WATER CREDITS.

The message pulsed across every wall.

Mara stood at the south gate with a dull spear in her hands and a ration tag clipped to her collar. Three meals if she survived. One meal sent to her brother regardless. That had been enough to make her sign.

Across the arena, her opponent emerged through steam and chain-link doors.

A man older than her. Heavyset. Exhausted before the fight even began.

The screens flashed his record overhead.

TOM ARDEN
7 VICTORIES
DEPENDENTS: 2

The crowd reacted to that. Not sympathy. Interest. Dependents made people desperate.

A siren sounded.

The floor between them split open mechanically, raising crates of weapons no one maintained properly anymore. Rusted machetes. Pipe clubs. A hatchet with half its handle wrapped in electrical tape.

Mara ignored them. Keeping the spear gave her distance.

Tom chose the hatchet.

For several seconds neither moved. The arena hated that. The crowd started stamping their feet in unison, thousands of shoes hammering metal benches.

FIGHT.
FIGHT.
FIGHT.

Mara circled first.

Tom came at her suddenly, faster than she expected. The hatchet clipped the shaft of her spear hard enough to jar her wrists numb. He pressed close, trying to get inside her reach. She stumbled backward over cracked tile, barely twisting away as the blade slammed sparks from the ground.

The audience roared now.

Not because of skill. Because they wanted panic.

Tom swung again. Mara blocked high, wood splintering. He shoved into her with his shoulder and both of them crashed beside one of the old rail tracks embedded in the floor.

Up close, she could see how starving he was.

His eyes flicked once to her ration tag.

Then to the cameras.

He wasn’t fighting her anymore. He was fighting the thought of two children waiting at home.

He charged again with a raw shout.

Mara reacted on instinct.

She sidestepped and drove the broken spear forward with both hands.

The jagged end punched through his chest beneath the collarbone. The force of his movement carried him farther onto it. His hatchet slipped from his fingers and clattered across the concrete.

The arena fell strangely quiet.

Tom looked down at the spear lodged in him with confusion more than pain. He tried once to speak, but blood filled the space where words should have been. His knees gave out slowly.

Mara lowered him to the ground because the cameras liked mercy almost as much as violence.

Above them, the screens exploded with color.

VICTOR CONFIRMED.
RATION DISPENSATION AUTHORIZED.

The crowd applauded automatically.

Somewhere high overhead, behind mirrored glass, officials in clean uniforms watched another citizen earn the right to eat for one more week.

The engine screamed as the sedan shot between lanes, tires skimming painted lines slick with rain and oil. Horns erupted on every side. A delivery van swerved hard enough to climb the curb, scattering pedestrians who had been waiting to cross. Through the shattered rear window, Mara twisted in her seat, one hand gripping the frame while the other leveled a pistol at the black SUVs bearing down behind them.

The first shot cracked like a whip inside the car. Muzzle flash lit her face in brief orange pulses. The recoil jolted up her arm, but adrenaline drowned out everything except movement and speed. Another round punched into the windshield of the lead SUV, spiderwebbing the glass. The driver behind it jerked sideways, clipping a taxi hard enough to send it spinning across two lanes.

People screamed on the sidewalks. A cyclist abandoned his bike and dove behind a mailbox as the chase tore past. Mara caught flashes of terrified faces through windows they nearly sideswiped: a mother shielding her child in the back seat of a compact car, an elderly man frozen halfway through the crosswalk, a bus driver leaning on the horn as vehicles scattered ahead of the chaos.

Their own driver yanked the wheel left. The sedan threaded a gap barely wider than the mirrors, metal shrieking as they scraped a truck. Mara nearly lost her balance, shoulder slamming against the door. Her pulse hammered so violently it blurred her vision. Every second stretched thin and sharp. If she stopped firing, the SUVs would box them in. If she kept firing, one missed shot could hit someone who had nothing to do with any of it.

She fired again anyway.

The bullet shattered the pursuing SUV’s headlight. Sparks burst beneath its tires as it fishtailed, clipping a parked car and sending glass spraying across the street. Pedestrians scattered in panic. Somewhere behind the roar of engines and gunfire came the sound of another crash — heavy, final, unavoidable.

Mara’s chest tightened for half a heartbeat, then the driver accelerated harder, and the city became a tunnel of flashing lights, near misses, and consequences piling up too fast to count.

Mara stood in the parking garage long after the office lights had gone dark, staring at the black sedan in the corner space. Victor Hale’s car always looked polished enough to belong to someone cleaner than he was. The shine annoyed her most.

Three months earlier, her brother had sat in a courtroom while Victor calmly explained away the missing safety reports, the altered inspections, the shortcuts that collapsed an entire scaffolding line. Four workers injured. One dead. Victor walked free with a bonus and a promotion. Her brother, the site engineer who tried to report him, lost his license and his career.

Mara remembered the expression Victor wore outside the courthouse: mild irritation, as if the whole thing had merely delayed his lunch.

Now she crouched beside the sedan with trembling hands and a wrench tucked into her coat pocket. Every echo in the garage sounded like a warning. Every second stretched.

She told herself this was balance.

Not murder. Not really.

Victor had made his choices already. He had signed papers he knew were false. He had buried evidence. He had smiled while families emptied savings accounts to pay hospital bills. If the world refused to stop him, then the world had delegated the task to someone else.

To her.

That thought frightened her because it sounded reasonable.

Mara imagined tomorrow’s headlines. Tragic accident. Executive killed in brake failure. People would shake their heads for a day, maybe two. No one would mention the welder who died screaming beneath twisted metal because Victor approved defective supports. No one would connect the events except Mara herself.

A trade. One life for another.

Except it was never that clean, and she knew it.

Her father used to say revenge was a story people told themselves so they wouldn’t have to call it grief. Standing in the cold concrete dark, Mara finally understood what he meant. She didn’t want justice anymore. Justice would have required courts, confessions, consequences. What she wanted was for Victor to feel fear in the final seconds, the same helpless panic he had outsourced to strangers.

She reached toward the wheel well, then stopped.

In her mind she saw not Victor, but an unnamed driver on the highway beside him. A mother in another lane. A teenager crossing a street. Revenge widened like cracks in ice; you never knew where it would stop.

The wrench slipped from her hand and clattered loudly across the cement.

Mara stared at the car a long time before turning away. Victor Hale would wake tomorrow still breathing, still guilty, still protected by the same crooked machinery that had failed everyone else.

But she would not become another part of it.

Branches clawed at Mara’s face as she ran, the forest swallowing every direction into the same suffocating black. Wet leaves slid beneath her boots. Roots reached for her ankles like hands in the dark. Somewhere behind her, something moved between the trees with impossible patience.

Not crashing.
Not stumbling.

Following.

Her lungs burned. Each breath dragged cold air deep enough to hurt. She dared a glance over her shoulder and saw nothing except trunks packed tightly together and strips of pale fog drifting low across the ground.

That was worse.

The silence stretched until she could hear only her own ragged breathing and the frantic hammering of blood in her ears.

Then came the sound.

A sharp twang snapped through the trees.

Mara didn’t understand it at first. Her body did before her mind did. She threw herself sideways just as something sliced through the air beside her head with a vicious whistle.

A crossbow bolt.

It passed so close she felt the wind of it against her ear — a cold, razor-thin kiss — before it buried itself deep into the trunk ahead with a heavy thunk.

Mara hit the ground hard, mud soaking through her clothes. For a heartbeat she could only stare at the bolt quivering in the bark, black feathers trembling.

If she’d been half a step slower—

Another sound drifted through the dark. Footsteps. Measured. Unhurried.

Whoever hunted her knew they didn’t need to rush.

Panic surged hot and electric through her chest. She scrambled up and ran again, weaving between the trees, trying to make herself small, unpredictable, impossible to hit. Every shadow became the outline of a drawn weapon. Every creak overhead sounded like death taking aim.

Then the forest fell silent again.

That silence was the worst part.

Because somewhere in it, unseen eyes were watching her.

By noon the shouting had sunk into the earth.
Smoke dragged its sleeves across the field
and settled in the furrows.
Broken wheels leaned into the grass.
A horse, stiff with flies,
held one white eye to the sun.

The dead lay where the morning left them,
hands open,
as though sleep had interrupted
some unfinished argument.
Mud dried on their boots.
Buttons dulled.
One man’s cap had filled with rainwater
and a yellow wasp climbed out of it
like a thought returning.

Above them,
the crows descended in patient angles,
black scraps loosening from the clouds.
They did not hurry.
They knew the silence
would keep.

At the edge of the ditch
beetles worked beneath a torn flag,
dragging brightness into the dark.
Ants entered sleeves and collars,
disappearing into the still republic
of flesh.
Green flies stitched the air together,
thread by shining thread.

Nothing prayed.
The guns had gone quiet enough
for small sounds to inherit the world:
the click of mandibles,
the tick of cooling metal,
wings rasping over open mouths.

Toward evening
the wind moved through the bodies
and lifted the hair from their foreheads
like a mother checking for fever.
No one rose.

Far off,
someone’s dog barked once,
then understood the distance.

Night came carefully.
The stars gathered above the field
without judgment.
And all through the dark,
the scavengers continued their tender labor,
returning each name
to the earth without speaking it.

The dog came out of the gray haze between collapsed cars without a sound at first, just a low shape moving with the caution of something that had learned pain from everything alive. Its ribs showed through mangy fur. One ear was torn to a stump. Its eyes locked onto the strip of dried meat hanging from the character’s hand with the same raw desperation burning in his own stomach.

For a second, neither moved.

Wind pushed ash along the cracked highway. Somewhere far off, metal groaned in the ruins of a dead building.

Then the dog lunged.

Its weight slammed into him hard enough to drive him onto his back. The meat flew from his grip and skidded across the pavement. Teeth snapped inches from his face, hot breath thick with rot and starvation. He shoved his forearm into the animal’s throat on instinct, feeling wiry muscle and jutting bones beneath filthy fur as the dog clawed at his chest.

He was starving enough that fear barely registered anymore.

Three days without real food had hollowed him out. His hands shook constantly. Every movement cost energy he didn’t have. The strip of meat wasn’t even enough for a full meal — maybe a few mouthfuls once boiled — but his body reacted to losing it like losing life itself.

The dog twisted free and darted for the food.

He grabbed a chunk of broken concrete and swung wildly. The first blow missed. The second caught the animal in the shoulder with a sickening thud. The dog yelped but didn’t retreat. Hunger had burned caution out of it too.

It turned on him again, snarling now, lips peeled back from yellow teeth.

They crashed together in the dirt beside the road, more like scavengers than living creatures. He drove his knee into its ribs. The dog bit into his sleeve and nearly reached flesh beneath. He could hear himself grunting, coughing, fighting with the last scraps of strength left in him. Every heartbeat hammered one thought through his skull:

Food. Food. Food.

The meat lay inches away in the grime.

When the dog lunged again, he caught its neck with both hands and slammed it against the pavement. The animal bucked violently, claws scraping his arms bloody. For a terrible moment he thought he would lose. Then exhaustion finally overtook the dog before it overtook him.

It went still except for ragged breathing.

He stayed there over it, trembling so badly he could barely move. The dog crawled backward at last, limping away into the ruins with a low whine.

He snatched the scrap of meat off the ground before it could disappear again.

His hands were slick with dirt and blood — some his, some not — but he tore into the food immediately, chewing before he even realized tears had started running down his face. The meat was tough, foul-tasting, barely enough to quiet the ache inside him.

But for tonight, he would not starve.

Rain hammered the roof of the abandoned ranger station hard enough to drown out the distant gunfire. Water leaked through the ceiling in cold, steady drips, pattering onto the warped wooden floorboards where Elias lay flat on his back, pale and shaking.

His hands were pressed against his own stomach, but blood kept squeezing through his fingers in dark, slick pulses.

“Don’t move,” Mara snapped.

“I’m trying not to.”

His voice cracked halfway through the sentence.

Mara dropped to her knees beside him and looked at the wound again. The bullet had entered low on the right side of his abdomen. The flesh around it was swollen and torn black-red beneath the blood. Every breath made the edges of the wound quiver wetly.

No med kit. No bandages. No morphine.

Just a hunting knife and a half-full bottle of whiskey.

Outside, another burst of rifle fire echoed through the trees.

“We don’t have time,” Elias whispered.

“Shut up.”

Mara grabbed the whiskey bottle with trembling fingers and unscrewed the cap with her teeth. The sharp smell filled the room instantly.

“This is going to hurt.”

“It already hurts.”

She poured whiskey directly into the wound.

Elias screamed.

His entire body arched off the floorboards. Blood and liquor spilled together down his side while he clawed at the wood hard enough to splinter it beneath his nails. The alcohol flushed pink for a second before turning dark again.

“Jesus Christ—”

“I know.”

Mara wiped the knife blade on her sleeve, then held it over the flame of a lantern for only a few seconds. Not enough to sterilize it properly. Just enough to make herself feel less helpless.

The bullet hadn’t gone through.

That was the problem.

She pressed one hand against his shoulder. “You move, you die.”

“Comforting.”

His face had gone gray with sweat. His teeth chattered violently despite the heat.

Mara pushed the knife into the wound.

Elias made a sound she had never heard from another human being before — not a scream, not a yell, but something animal and raw. His legs kicked against the floor. Blood welled immediately around the blade, hot and slippery across Mara’s hand.

“Hold still!”

“I CAN’T—”

“You have to!”

She widened the wound with short, brutal movements. Flesh resisted the blade with a sickening elasticity before giving way. Blood ran over her wrists. She could feel the heat of his body through it.

Elias gagged.

Then vomited onto the floor beside him.

The smell hit seconds later: whiskey, blood, bile, burned oil from the lantern.

Mara shoved two fingers into the opening, searching blindly.

Elias shrieked and grabbed her arm hard enough to bruise.

“I can feel it,” she said.

“Then get it out!”

Her fingertips brushed metal lodged deep inside torn tissue. The bullet was slick and stubborn, buried somewhere near the back muscle.

She dug harder.

Elias convulsed beneath her. Tears streamed sideways into his hair. Every breath came ragged and wet.

Then her fingers closed around the flattened slug.

She pulled.

The bullet came free with a thick rush of blood.

For one horrible second it poured out of him in a dark sheet, spilling across the floorboards and soaking Mara’s knees.

“No no no—”

The warehouse had been empty for years, its windows punched out like missing teeth, its metal siding warped by rain and neglect. To everyone else, it was an eyesore waiting to collapse. To him, it was a payout wrapped in dry timber and dust.

He stood across the street with his hands buried in his pockets, watching the first orange flicker take hold deep inside the building. At first it looked small, almost harmless. Then it crawled upward, finding beams and insulation and forgotten scraps left behind by time. The flames spread with hungry confidence, and he felt something tighten pleasantly in his chest as the darkness lit up.

There was a thrill in seeing something irreversible begin.

The fire moved faster than he expected, blooming through shattered windows in violent bursts of light. Smoke rolled into the sky in thick black columns. The old structure groaned as heat twisted steel and cracked ancient wood apart. He imagined the paperwork already moving through insurance offices, signatures and numbers replacing the building more efficiently than any demolition crew ever could.

People would call it tragic. Dangerous. Criminal.

But standing there, he felt detached from all of that. The destruction barely registered as destruction at all. The warehouse had already been dead in his mind. The fire simply erased the evidence.

Sirens wailed somewhere in the distance, still far enough away to sound unreal. He watched the flames pulse brighter, reflected in his eyes like a private celebration. The heat reached him even from across the street, dry and intense, carrying the scent of smoke and chemicals into the cold night air.

For a moment, he couldn’t look away.

The fire consumed without hesitation, without guilt. That was part of what fascinated him most: how quickly something solid became fragile, then ruin, then ash drifting upward into nothing. And underneath the excitement sat a colder thought, one he refused to examine too closely—that once you crossed a line like this, it became easier to imagine crossing another.

“You know what I find interesting?” the torturer asked quietly. “People think pain is the worst part.”

The captive kept their eyes fixed on the concrete floor. Their wrists ached against the restraints, but they refused to shift.

“It isn’t,” the torturer continued. “Pain is simple. Immediate. Honest. The worst part is anticipation. That moment where your mind starts bargaining with itself.”

Silence.

A chair scraped across the room. Deliberate. Slow.

“You’ve already started, haven’t you?”

The captive swallowed but said nothing.

The torturer sat down directly across from them. No mask. No raised voice. Just a patient expression that somehow made the room feel smaller.

“I know you think this is about loyalty,” they said. “Or principle. Maybe you’ve even convinced yourself the password matters more than you do.”

Still nothing.

“But every person has a limit. The body was designed that way. Nerves fail. Resolve erodes. Time stretches.” The torturer leaned forward slightly. “I don’t need you brave forever. I just need you tired.”

The captive finally looked up. “You’re wasting your time.”

“Maybe.” A faint shrug. “But it’s my time to waste.”

The torturer reached to the metal tray beside them. Instruments rested there in careful rows, untouched. The captive’s eyes flicked toward them despite themselves.

That earned the smallest hint of a smile.

“There it is,” the torturer said softly. “Not fear of pain. Fear of imagining it.”

“You think showing me tools changes anything?”

“No. The tools are theater.” The torturer folded their hands. “What changes people is uncertainty. You don’t know what comes next. You don’t know how long this lasts. Your mind will create worse things than I ever could.”

The captive tried to steady their breathing.

The torturer noticed.

“You’re calculating now. That’s good. Smart people calculate.” Their voice remained calm, almost conversational. “You’re wondering how much you can endure before talking. Whether you should hold out longer. Whether anyone is even coming for you.”

“They are.”

“Maybe.” Another shrug. “But hope is dangerous in rooms like this. It stretches suffering out.”

The captive clenched their jaw.

The torturer tilted their head. “Do you know why I haven’t touched you yet?”

No answer.

“Because right now, you still believe you’re in control. The moment pain begins, the conversation changes. Every second afterward becomes about stopping the next second.”

The room hummed faintly with fluorescent lights.

“You can avoid all of that,” the torturer said. “A single password. That’s all.”

The captive laughed once, dry and strained. “And then what? You let me go?”

“No.” The honesty landed harder than a threat. “But what happens afterward depends greatly on how long this takes.”

The captive looked away again.

The torturer stood slowly. “Here’s what I think. I think you came in prepared for heroics. People always do. They imagine themselves defiant. Noble.” A pause. “But nobility fades remarkably fast when the body realizes the danger is real.”

A long silence followed.

Then the torturer picked up one of the instruments. Not using it. Just holding it where it could be seen.

The captive’s breathing changed again.

“There it is,” the torturer murmured. “That moment. Your imagination is doing the work for me.”

The captive shut their eyes.

“Tell me the password.”

“No.”

The torturer nodded once, almost respectfully.

“Then we continue.”

The first thing he noticed was the silence.

Not the absence of sound—the building groaned around him, pipes shrieking somewhere in the walls—but the unnatural silence from downstairs. No footsteps. No voices. No warning.

Then came the smell.

Smoke rolled under the office door in thick gray ribbons, curling across the floor like something alive. Daniel lurched from his chair, coughing immediately as the first breath scraped down his throat like hot sandpaper. He grabbed the handle.

Locked.

His pulse stumbled.

“No,” he whispered, then louder, slamming his shoulder against the door. “No—!”

The metal frame rattled but held firm. Outside, somewhere below, flames crackled with growing appetite. He could hear them climbing.

Marcus.

The realization hit harder than the smoke. The strange phone call. The missing night guard. The way Marcus had smiled that afternoon, cold and patient, saying, “Some debts close permanently.”

Daniel backed away from the door, panic flooding his limbs so fast it made him dizzy. He tore off his jacket and wrapped it around his hand before trying the knob again. The metal burned even through the fabric.

Another cough doubled him over. This one brought tears to his eyes.

The smoke thickened with terrifying speed, swallowing the ceiling first, then lowering inch by inch. The room dimmed into a choking haze lit orange from beneath the doorframe. Heat pressed against his skin from every direction now, dry and merciless.

He stumbled toward the windows.

Ten stories down.

The street below looked impossibly far away, warped behind soot-streaked glass. He pounded against the pane anyway, shouting until his voice cracked raw. No one looked up. Sirens wailed faintly in the distance, too far away.

The fire reached the hallway outside.

A roar thundered beyond the door, followed by a violent boom that shook the room hard enough to knock him sideways. The overhead lights exploded in sparks. Suddenly the smoke became black, oily, impossible to see through.

Daniel dropped to his knees instinctively, gasping near the floor where the air was marginally clearer. Every inhale still seared his lungs. His skin prickled painfully. The heat had become unbearable now—blistering against his face, his hands.

The windows began to crack.

One sharp line splintered across the nearest pane.

Then another.

Daniel stared at them through watering eyes as the glass bowed inward from the pressure and heat outside. Somewhere beneath the roar of the flames, he heard another sound.

Footsteps.

Slow.

Approaching from the other side of the locked office door.

The city was all sodium light and bad decisions, the kind of place where a man could disappear long before they buried him. Rain stitched itself across the hotel window in crooked little lines. Fifteenth floor. Good sightline. Bad karma.

The rifle lay in pieces across the table like the bones of a mechanical saint. Clean metal. Matte black. Nothing flashy. Flashy gets you remembered.

I snapped the first section into place and listened for the click. Precise. Quiet. Permanent.

Funny thing about this kind of work: nobody hires you to pull a trigger. They hire you to carry a certainty all the way to the end. The trigger’s just punctuation.

The receiver settled into the stock. Hands steady. Always steady. I used to think that meant something about me. Discipline. Professionalism. Maybe honor, if you squinted hard enough through a bottle. But a snake keeps steady, too, right before it bites.

I checked the barrel alignment under the dim lamp. No rush. Rushing is for amateurs and guilty men.

People imagine killers as wolves, all teeth and appetite. Truth is, most of us are accountants. We measure distance. Wind. Time. Regret. We subtract one heartbeat from the world and wait for the balance sheet to settle.

The target’s photograph sat beside the ashtray. Middle-aged. Expensive haircut. Smile like a locked safe. According to the file, he sold children to wars that didn’t officially exist. According to another file, he donated hospitals to cities he poisoned. Men like him built monuments out of contradictions.

Did he deserve it?

That question always arrives late, like a drunk relative stumbling into church after the sermon’s over.

I slid the bolt into place and worked it once. Smooth action. Smooth enough to make a priest nervous.

There are rules in this line of work, though nobody writes them down. Don’t kill for anger. Don’t kill for pleasure. Don’t ever convince yourself you’re the hero. The minute you start believing that, you stop noticing the blood on your hands.

I used to notice it all the time.

Now I just notice whether my fingers shake.

Outside, traffic crawled below in red and white streams. Every car carrying somebody home, or away from it. Somewhere down there a couple was fighting over dinner. Somebody was kissing somebody they shouldn’t. Somebody was finding out their biopsy came back bad. The world kept moving while men like me paused it for individuals.

One breath. One squeeze. One obituary drafted before impact.

I mounted the scope and stared through the glass at nothing. Empty rooftop. Neon signs buzzing like dying insects. The crosshairs floated over the city, searching for a reason.

There never is one.

That’s the secret nobody tells you.

Not revenge. Not justice. Not money.

Just momentum.

A man takes one bad job because he’s desperate. Then another because he’s trapped. Then another because he’s good at it. One day he wakes up in a rented room with a rifle worth more than his childhood home, wondering at what exact moment he traded his soul for professional standards.

The rain got heavier.

I checked my watch.

Three minutes.

The target would appear soon, wrapped in security and confidence, protected from everything except distance. Distance is the oldest betrayal there is. It lets you pretend you’re not really there when it happens.

But you are there.

You hear the shot inside yourself long after the city swallows the sound.

Rainwater dripped from the fire escapes in uneven rhythms, tapping the lids of overflowing dumpsters and turning the alley into a ribbon of black pavement and reflected neon. The city hummed somewhere beyond the brick walls, distant traffic and muffled music leaking through cracked windows, but back here everything felt sealed off, airless.

Marlowe kept his hands in his coat pockets to stop them from shaking.

“You said you had the cash,” he muttered.

Vic stood opposite him beneath a flickering security light, jaw working, one eye swollen from something that had happened earlier in the week—or earlier that night. He held a small duffel bag tucked tight against his side.

“I said I had most of it.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

Vic glanced toward the mouth of the alley. Nervous. Calculating. “You’re still getting paid.”

“After what I risked?” Marlowe stepped closer. “No.”

The silence stretched thin.

Water dripped somewhere behind them.

Vic’s expression hardened first. “You don’t get to threaten me.”

Marlowe barked a humorless laugh. “Threaten you? You came begging to me.”

The bag hit the pavement with a dull thud. Vic’s hand disappeared inside his jacket.

Marlowe saw the motion too late.

The knife flashed silver under the dying light.

“Vic—”

Then they were crashing into each other, shoes slipping on wet concrete. Marlowe caught Vic’s wrist with both hands, forcing the blade away from his throat as they slammed shoulder-first into the wall. Brick scraped skin through fabric. Vic smelled like cigarettes and cold sweat.

“Give it up!” Marlowe shouted through gritted teeth.

Vic snarled and twisted hard. The knife jerked downward.

A sudden punch of impact landed low in Marlowe’s side.

For half a second it didn’t even register as pain—just pressure, strange and heavy. Then heat spread through his ribs in a violent wave. His grip faltered.

He sucked in breath too fast and nearly choked on it.

Vic yanked the blade free.

That was worse.

The pain arrived sharp and deep, like something tearing open beneath the skin. Marlowe folded instinctively, one arm clamping against his side. Warmth spilled between his fingers immediately, soaking through his shirt despite the cold rain.

The alley tilted.

Vic shoved him backward. Marlowe hit the pavement hard enough to rattle his teeth. The world narrowed to wet asphalt, blurred neon reflections, and the burning throb pulsing through his torso with every heartbeat.

Vic stared at him for a moment, chest heaving, knife trembling in his hand as if he hadn’t expected things to go this far.

Then voices echoed somewhere near the street.

Vic grabbed the duffel bag and ran.

Marlowe tried to push himself upright, but another stab of pain dropped him back down. His side felt hot and numb at once, fingers slick and useless against the wound. Rain hit his face in cold pinpricks while the sounds of the city rolled on, indifferent.
